WORRY GUIDE — WORK

When you're torn about accepting a job offer

The news of an offer should make you happy, yet when you go to reply "I accept," your hand stops. A small catch about the conditions, lingering attachment to your current job, the feeling that "there might be a better company." Being torn over an offer comes from the overlap of not wanting to let this chance slip, and the fear of committing to it. On this page, we'll look at ways to take that indecision apart, and tarot cards that reflect each angle.

POINT 01

What's making this hard

Many people think, before receiving an offer, "if I pass, I'll decide" — yet once it actually comes to deciding, the indecision appears. What's behind it is resistance to losing the freedom to choose. Accept, and the other possibilities close; decline, and this chance won't come back. Discontent with conditions such as pay and work location also gets mixed together with hopes for the work itself and the people, making it hard to see even for yourself where you're catching. And the closer the reply deadline, the more impatience joins in. Start by writing out, separately, your discontent with the conditions, your hopes for the environment, your attachment to your current job, and your anxiety about the future, and check what is pulling you the most.

POINT 02

How to sort it out

The key to sorting it out is to divide your "reasons to decline" and "reasons to accept" into things that can change and things that can't. Pay and start date can sometimes move through negotiation, but you can't change a business's prospects or a company's culture yourself. An offer is also "a settled evaluation of who you are now." Picture concretely where you'll be in a year if you stay at your current job, and in a year if you move, and compare which would give you the experience you need now. If the material isn't in place by the deadline, asking to extend the reply deadline is another option. Deciding with the material in place, rather than deciding in a rush, leaves less regret.

POINT 03

How to read the cards

When you're torn over an offer, cards that reflect "an opportunity being offered," "eyes that weigh the conditions," and "a viewpoint looking one step ahead" can offer clues.

The Ace of Pentacles stands for the practical chance itself, offered right in front of you.

Justice shows the stance of weighing conditions and feelings fairly, and choosing on grounds you can accept.

The Two of Wands is a card for the stage of looking out from where you are now over a new landscape, and making a plan. Look at whether the card you drew leans toward "taking the opportunity" or toward "weighing it," and check which viewpoint you're missing right now.

POINT 04

Questions to ask yourself

Try answering the following questions. Is the condition you're catching on something that would move if you negotiated, or something that touches the company's essence? Can you concretely picture yourself working at this company? If you declined, what kind of company would you end up looking for next? Is your reason for staying at your current job to move forward, or to avoid change? Which choice could the you of one year from now say of, "I'm glad I decided back then"? If there's a question that's hard to answer, that's the point to confirm before the deadline.

CARDS

Cards connected to this decision

  • Ace of Pentacles

    A card that stands for the practical chance itself, offered right in front of you.

  • Justice

    The stance of weighing conditions and feelings fairly, and choosing with grounds.

  • Two of Wands

    The stage of looking out from your current place over the landscape ahead, and making your next plan.

  • Two of Swords

    It reflects a state in which you can't decide either way and are holding the judgment in reserve.

  • Seven of Pentacles

    A viewpoint for calmly weighing your efforts and their fruits so far, and deciding whether to continue or rethink.

Accept, or think a little more? Why not line up not only pay and conditions, but also whether you can picture yourself working there?
